title: Disinformation and misinformation in epilepsy: An analysis of multiplatform short-form social media video content.
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 562 short-form videos retrieved with the search term 'epilepsy' on TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts (URLs captured 8 June 2025). Three evaluators independently coded each video for whether it contained disinformation/misinformation, defined as 'information in contradiction to clinical recommendations'. The paper reports the share of videos so classified overall (18.1%) and separately for each platform (TikTok 31.7%, Instagram Reels 16.8%, YouTube Shorts 8%) - CONTENT prevalence with explicit denominators.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language search intended to capture international content (authors in Canada)
estimates.platform: TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts combined
estimates.date: URLs recorded 8 June 2025; videos published 12 February 2016 to 5 June 2025 (median 22 August 2024)
estimates.measure_type: % of epilepsy short-form videos (three platforms pooled) classified as containing disinformation or misinformation
estimates.denominator: 562 epilepsy videos retained after exclusions (from 750 URLs, 250 per platform; 73 unavailable, 114 excluded as off-topic, duplicate or animal-only)
estimates.definition: Videos classified as containing disinformation/misinformation if they contained information in contradiction to clinical recommendations (e.g. promotion of unverified treatments, confusion between epilepsy and functional neurological disorders without clinical nuance, claims presented without scientific basis as medical advice); depicting a functional/dissociative seizure without explicitly branding it as epileptic did NOT count
estimates.misinfo_def: "Disinformation refers to the deliberate dissemination of false information with the intent to enforce a certain agenda. Misinformation, on the other hand, refers to the involuntary dissemination of such false information." (the two were not distinguished in coding)
estimates.source_quote: A total of 102 videos (18.1%; 95% CI: 14.9–21.3) were clas- sified as containing disinformation or misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results 3.3 'Disinformation and misinformation analysis', p. 5-6 (the 'clas- sified' break is the PDF's line-break hyphenation); the Abstract restates it as 'In total, 102 videos (18.1% [14.9-21.3]) were classified as containing disinformation/misinformation'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three evaluators (a student living with epilepsy, an adult-neurology resident, and an epileptologist) independently watched every video and recorded yes/no for disinformation/misinformation on a standardised form; if the senior evaluator plus one other agreed, that verdict stood; if the two junior evaluators agreed against the senior, all three met to rewatch and decide. Interrater agreement 83.5% (95% CI: 80.6-86.0).
estimates.moderator_quote: We searched TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts for epilepsy short-form videos using the free text term “epilepsy.” We chose such a broad, English search term to capture the widest and most international range of videos concerning epilepsy. For this search, we used a new, blank account. ... A total of 750 video URLs were recorded, 250 from each social media platform ... This URL recording phase was conducted on June 8th, 2025 | Videos were classified as containing disinformation/misinformation if they contained information in contradiction to clinical recommendations.
estimates.notes: POOLED row. The three platform rows below are the components of this same 562-video sample (53 + 33 + 16 = 102), so a pooling analysis must take EITHER this row OR the three platform rows, never both. Internal inconsistency in the paper: the Abstract says 563 videos remained with 196 from Instagram Reels, while Results and Table 3 say 562 with 195; the percentages match the 562/195 denominators, so those are used here. Numerator counts by platform are not printed and are derivable only by multiplication, so they are not treated as verbatim.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) FDS analysis NOT extracted: 115 videos showed a clinical spell and 78 (67.8%; 95% CI 59.3-76.4) were judged likely functional/dissociative seizures rather than epileptic seizures (Instagram Reels 23/26 = 88.5%, TikTok 49/72 = 68.1%, YouTube Shorts 6/17 = 35.3%). This is a share of items judged by an epileptologist against clinical ground truth, but the authors explicitly state that depicting an FDS is NOT counted as disinformation/misinformation unless the video brands it as an epileptic seizure, so it is not a falsity share; it is also judged by a single evaluator. An adjudicator wanting a broader 'misrepresentation' construct could add it as a borderline row. 2) Content-category splits of the misinformation rate (medical advice 72.7% [46.4-99], personal experience 25.1%, stigmatization 20%, oblique reference 11.8%, educational 10.4%, joke/entertainment 2.6%) are sub-splits of the same 102-video numerator and are not the paper's headline, so they were not rowed. 3) Content-category prevalences (personal experience 45.3%, educational 35.7%, etc.) are topic categories, not falsity. 4) Comparison figures cited from other studies ('approximately half of epilepsy content on TikTok was misleading', 55% FDS on TikTok) are from elsewhere and excluded by R8. 5) Unresolved internal inconsistency: Abstract 563 videos / 196 Instagram vs Results and Table 3 562 / 195.

rob.design: Cross-sectional multiplatform video content analysis. Frame: native search for the free-text term 'epilepsy' on TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts from a new blank account (to suppress personalisation), 250 URLs per platform captured by in-house Python on 8 June 2025; 73 videos unavailable at analysis, 114 excluded (85 off-topic, 17 animal-only, 12 duplicate), leaving 562 (Results) / 563 (Abstract). Coding: three evaluators of differing expertise (student with epilepsy, neurology resident, epileptologist) independently coded misinformation (yes/no) and content category on a standardised Excel form; senior-plus-one adjudication rule with joint rewatch for junior-vs-senior splits; categories retained only when at least two evaluators assigned them. Reliability: interrater agreement 83.5% (95% CI 80.6-86.0) with Wilson intervals; no kappa. Analysis in R 4.5.2 with 95% CIs. Ethics waived (public data). Stated limitations: fewer than the planned 250 videos per platform, blank-account search not generalisable to personalised feeds, disinformation and misinformation could not be separated, FDS-vs-epileptic judgement by the senior evaluator alone, and subjectivity of content categorisation.
